newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian analysts debate another rate cut.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian analysts debate another rate cut.

text.p: Australia had to wait 1-1/2 years for a change in monetary policy, but in the space of three months there have been two easings and the question now is: "Will there be a third in this cycle?"

Official interest rates were cut by a 1/2 point to 6.50 percent last Wednesday, a move that had generally been expected, although some quarters had been looking for a bigger reduction and believe the case for a further easing already exists.
A Reuters survey of economists taken on Friday gave a median 50 percent probability of another rate reduction.
Twenty four out of the 29 economists polled said that if there was a further cut it would be in the first quarter of next year and probably a further 50 basis points reduction.

"The soft economy and ongoing weak state of the labour market as we turn the corner in 1997, in conjunction with further improving inflation and broad-based wages growth is likely to continue to neutralise any residual fears that the RBA have about the size of enterprise deals being struck," said John Peters, senior economist at Westpac Banking Group.
Westpac gave a 90 percent chance of a 50 basis point easing in the March quarter in the survey.

Wage growth pressures from enterprise bargaining agreements are seen as one of the main hurdles holding back the RBA from a further easing, and it will also be monitoring business capital investment plans, data of which are due later this month.

However, low inflation projections and high unemployment are seen as key elements to a further policy easing and March 1997 bill futures are already indicating a cash rate of 6.20 percent when the contract expires on March 13.
But, at the other end of the scale, economists at Rothschild Australia believe there is only a 25 percent chance of a rate cut in December, and not much more in the New Year.

"Our central forecast is that we have seen the low for cash rates this time around. Growth of 2.5 percent in 1996/97 does not demand cash rates at the levels seen coming out of the last recession," Rothschild said in a report.

However, the debate over a further interest rate cut is not just in the financial markets -- the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) said on Monday that the RBA must aim for higher economic growth if unemployment is to be brought down.
"To maintain a faster rate of growth, interest rates must come down further and remain low," the business group said.

The unemployment rate, a major concern of the RBA when it first cut rates in July from 7.50 percent, rose to 8.8 percent in the October labour force report released last week from 8.7 percent in September.

However, Rothschild economists argue that the Australian economy should strengthen in 1997 and that the RBA will be wary that cutting aggressively at this stage of the cycle will turn out to be pro-cyclical in that a stimulus will have its greatest impact at a time when the economy is already strengthening.
